item.title: New York Times and Other Publishers Sue Brave Over AI Scraping and Paywall Bypass
item.description:
New York Times and Other Publishers Sue Brave Over AI Scraping and Paywall Bypass

🔍 Overview

Several major news organizations, including The New York Times, have filed lawsuits against Brave Software, the company behind the Brave web browser. The suits allege that Brave unlawfully scraped copyrighted articles to create a searchable “Brave Index,” then sold access to that index to generative‑AI firms while also allowing users to bypass paywalls.

📜 Allegations

  • Brave copied and distributed publishers’ copyrighted content without permission.
  • The company offered a “Paywall blocker” that lets users access premium articles for free.
  • Brave monetized its index of scraped sites by giving AI companies paid access to real‑time online content.
  • Publishers were not compensated for the alleged copying, distribution, or the paywall‑bypass feature.

🤖 AI Companies Involved

AI Company Alleged Use of Brave Index
Anthropic Trains models and/or responds to user queries using the indexed content
Perplexity Trains models and/or responds to user queries using the indexed content
Mistral Trains models and/or responds to user queries using the indexed content
xAI Trains models and/or responds to user queries using the indexed content
Cohere Trains models and/or responds to user queries using the indexed content

📣 Statements

  • “While we believe in the ethical and responsible use and development of AI, Brave has flouted established copyright law and ignored repeated requests by The Times to stop its infringing conduct,” said Graham James, NYT spokesperson (quoted to The Verge).
  • “We filed this lawsuit to hold Brave accountable for stealing our content to power its own products and to provide it to some of the most prominent and well‑resourced generative AI companies in the world,” the NYT statement continued.
  • Attorney Steven Lieberman, representing the New York Daily News, Chicago Tribune, and Orlando Sentinel, said: “AI giants are now desperate to avoid getting caught red‑handed stealing news from publishers, so Brave Software is selling them a back door to the journalism they know they have no right to.”
  • “Buying stolen goods secondhand doesn’t make them legitimate. Brave must be held responsible for laundering pirated reporting for the AI industry,” added Lieberman.

📅 Update (Nov 2)

The lawsuit filed by the New York Daily News, Chicago Tribune, and Orlando Sentinel was clarified to be a separate action from the NYT case. The attorney’s statement on behalf of those three publications was also added.

All statements and facts are drawn directly from the reported complaints and public comments.

#NYT #Brave #AI #Copyright #Legal

Source: The New York Times sues Brave web browser for AI scraping and bypassing paywalls

item.title: Shivon Zilis Announces Breakup with Elon Musk Amid AI Portfolio Testimony
item.description:
Shivon Zilis Announces Breakup with Elon Musk Amid AI Portfolio Testimony

Shivon Zilis used X to announce that she and Elon Musk, the father of her four children, have broken up. The post was a quote‑tweet of a Big Tech Alert notice that Musk had stopped following her, and she added her own reflection on the sudden change.

🔍 Overview

  • Zilis posted the breakup on X, quoting Big Tech Alert that Elon Musk no longer follows her.
  • She wrote, “It’s hard to go from in love to let go in a week with no warning, but that’s just how it is sometimes.”
  • The announcement comes after a high‑profile trial in which Zilis testified about her work across Musk’s AI interests.

🤖 Role in Musk’s AI Portfolio

  • Zilis told the court she worked across Musk’s entire AI portfolio: Tesla, Neuralink, and OpenAI.
  • She described her workload as 80‑to‑100‑hour weeks, saying she was there “to go find bottlenecks and solve them.”
  • She served on OpenAI’s board while giving birth to twins, keeping the parentage of the children secret at the time.
  • Zilis only informed coworkers that the children’s father was a competitor in 2022, after Business Insider reported court documents naming Musk.

⚖️ Legal Context

  • During the trial, Zilis denied under oath that she was Musk’s chief of staff.
  • Musk testified that she was his chief of staff, a remark that drew loud laughter from the courtroom gallery.
  • The lawsuit involved Musk suing Sam Altman over Musk’s donations to OpenAI, with Zilis’s testimony focused on her AI‑related work for Musk.

❤️ Personal Statements

  • Zilis praised Musk in her breakup post: “I feel happy that I got to show Elon how it feels to be deeply understood, nurtured, and peacefully loved with stability and gentleness.”
  • She added, “Given the tumultuous nature of his early life … I wanted him to feel the deepest and most stable form of love this world can provide.”
  • She concluded, “I’ve loved him more than life itself and he’s taught me 100 lifetimes of knowledge… we created four beautiful little loves of my life.”
  • Recently, Zilis recommended Maye Musk’s memoir, calling the mother’s resilience a “beacon of resilience to draw inspiration from.”

📚 Related Personal Dynamics

  • Elon Musk is known to have 14 children.
  • Another mother of his children, Ashley St. Clair, rejected a $40 million NDA and is suing Musk over his chatbot Grok, which allegedly created deep‑fake nudes of her.
  • Former partner Grimes described pregnancy as “sacrificing your body and your freedom” and sued Musk to establish a parental relationship, even posting (and later deleting) a tweet asking Shivon to unblock her and demanding a response from Musk’s biographer.

#ElonMusk #ShivonZilis #OpenAI #AI

Source: Breaking up (with Elon Musk) is hard to do

item.title: Australian Government Sets $100 Million Penalty for Big Tech Digital Duty of Care
item.description:
Australian Government Sets $100 Million Penalty for Big Tech Digital Duty of Care

The Australian government has established a $100 million penalty for big tech companies that breach their digital duty of care.

⚙️ Key details

  • Penalty Amount: $100 million for breaches of digital duty of care.
  • Legal Basis: Communications Minister Anika Wells stated that the question of fines was “drafted around Australian consumer law.”

💡 Why it matters

Communications Minister Anika Wells has expressed skepticism regarding the effectiveness of financial penalties for the world’s wealthiest corporations:

  • Wells stated, “No particular figure that we mandate in Australia is going to be enough for the world’s richest companies.”
  • Wells noted that “there is no fine large enough to curb the behaviour of big tech companies.”
  • As an example of the scale of corporate payments, Wells said, “Meta just unblushingly paid $US18 billion ($25 billion) in a settlement a few weeks ago.”

#BigTech #Australia #DigitalRegulation #TechPolicy

Source: Australian news live updates: Anthropic CEO calls for global AI slowdown
